chapters.title: The Big Bang
chapters.tease: Everything you can see, and everything you are made of, was once smaller than an atom.

chapters.title: Galaxies
chapters.tease: The light from the Andromeda Galaxy set off before modern humans existed.

chapters.title: Stars
chapters.tease: The oxygen in every breath you take was forged inside a star that died before the Sun was born.

chapters.title: The Sun
chapters.tease: Every second the Sun turns about four million tonnes of its own mass into pure energy.

chapters.title: The Planets
chapters.tease: If the Sun were a front door, Earth would be a pea 200 metres away and Neptune six kilometres off.

chapters.title: The Moon
chapters.tease: The Moon is drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 centimetres a year, roughly as fast as fingernails grow.

chapters.title: Black Holes
chapters.tease: Squeeze the whole Earth down to the size of a marble and it would become a black hole.

chapters.title: Comets and Asteroids
chapters.tease: In 2022 humans deliberately crashed a spacecraft into an asteroid and changed its orbit.

chapters.title: Exoplanets
chapters.tease: There are probably more planets in the Milky Way than there are stars.

chapters.title: Exploring Space
chapters.tease: Space is only about an hour's drive away, if your car could point straight up.

chapters.title: Inside the Earth
chapters.tease: The deepest hole ever drilled reached 12 km. The centre of the Earth lies 6,371 km down.

chapters.title: Plate Tectonics
chapters.tease: The Atlantic Ocean is still widening by a few centimetres every year.

chapters.title: Volcanoes
chapters.tease: Measured from the seabed, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is over 10,000 metres tall, higher than Everest.

chapters.title: Earthquakes
chapters.tease: Each step up the magnitude scale releases about 32 times more energy than the one below.

chapters.title: Rocks and Minerals
chapters.tease: Every pebble is a stage in a cycle: melted, worn away, buried, baked and melted again.

chapters.title: The Water Cycle
chapters.tease: A water molecule spends about nine days in the sky, but can spend thousands of years in the deep sea.

chapters.title: Oceans
chapters.tease: Mount Everest could sink into the Mariana Trench with over 2 km of water to spare.

chapters.title: Weather
chapters.tease: A bolt of lightning heats the air to around 30,000°C, about five times hotter than the Sun's surface.

chapters.title: Climate
chapters.tease: Carbon dioxide in the air is now higher than at any time in at least 800,000 years.

chapters.title: Biomes
chapters.tease: Rainforests cover around 6% of the land, yet may hold half of all land species.

chapters.title: What Is Life?
chapters.tease: Fire grows, feeds and breathes oxygen, yet it is not alive. A mule cannot breed, yet it is.

chapters.title: Cells
chapters.tease: Every human began as one cell, which divided until it became around 30 trillion.

chapters.title: Evolution
chapters.tease: In one drought on one Galápagos island, finch beaks measurably changed in a single generation.

chapters.title: The Tree of Life
chapters.tease: Fungi are closer relatives of animals than of plants, and whales are cousins of hippos.

chapters.title: Microbes
chapters.tease: Bacteria hold about 35 times as much carbon as every animal on Earth put together.

chapters.title: Plants
chapters.tease: A tree is built mostly from thin air: carbon dioxide turned solid by sunlight.

chapters.title: Invertebrates
chapters.tease: About 97 in every 100 known animal species have no backbone, and most of those are insects.

chapters.title: Vertebrates
chapters.tease: Your jaw began as the gill supports of a fish that swam more than 400 million years ago.

chapters.title: Dinosaurs
chapters.tease: T. rex lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus.

chapters.title: Ecosystems
chapters.tease: Only about a tenth of the energy at each step of a food chain reaches the next.

chapters.title: Building a Body
chapters.tease: You began as one cell a tenth of a millimetre wide. You are now around 37 trillion of them.

chapters.title: The Skeleton
chapters.tease: Over half of the body's 206 bones are in the hands and feet.

chapters.title: Muscles
chapters.tease: Muscle can only pull, never push, yet that single trick powers every move the body makes.

chapters.title: Heart and Blood
chapters.tease: The heart beats around 100,000 times a day, and it starts every beat by itself.

chapters.title: Lungs and Breathing
chapters.tease: Spread flat, the lungs' 480 million air sacs would cover around 70 square metres.

chapters.title: Digestion
chapters.tease: A meal's trip from mouth to exit takes one to three days, mostly in the large intestine.

chapters.title: The Brain
chapters.tease: The brain is 2% of body weight but burns about 20% of its energy, even at rest.

chapters.title: The Senses
chapters.tease: The brain never meets light or sound, only electrical pulses, and builds the world from them.

chapters.title: The Immune System
chapters.tease: The immune system is an army with no headquarters that remembers every enemy it has beaten.

chapters.title: DNA and Genes
chapters.tease: Four chemical letters, repeated 3.1 billion times, spell out the instructions for a human.

chapters.title: Atoms
chapters.tease: A full stop on this page is roughly a million atoms wide.

chapters.title: The Periodic Table
chapters.tease: Mendeleev left gaps for elements nobody had seen, and they turned up as forecast.

chapters.title: States of Matter
chapters.tease: On the summit of Everest, water boils at only about 70 °C.

chapters.title: Chemical Reactions
chapters.tease: No atom is ever created or destroyed in a reaction. They are only reshuffled.

chapters.title: Forces and Motion
chapters.tease: A rocket needs nothing to push against. It pushes on its own exhaust.

chapters.title: Gravity
chapters.tease: A fridge magnet beats the gravity of a whole planet, yet gravity builds the galaxies.

chapters.title: Energy
chapters.tease: Weight for weight, chocolate holds about five times more energy than TNT.

chapters.title: Electricity and Magnetism
chapters.tease: A spark and a compass needle turned out to be the same force wearing two faces.

chapters.title: Light and Sound
chapters.tease: Real explosions in space are silent: sound cannot cross a vacuum.

chapters.title: Relativity and Quantum
chapters.tease: Without Einstein's corrections, GPS would drift by about 10 km a day.

chapters.title: Simple Machines
chapters.tease: Every machine on Earth, from a tower crane to a tin opener, is built from six ancient ideas.

chapters.title: The Wheel
chapters.tease: People were sailing boats and smelting copper long before anyone thought to put a load on wheels.

chapters.title: The Printing Press
chapters.tease: A goldsmith's metal letters and a converted wine press turned books from treasures into everyday objects.

chapters.title: The Steam Engine
chapters.tease: One engineer's fix for a wasteful mine pump ended up powering factories, railways and cities.

chapters.title: Electric Power
chapters.tease: Every light switch connects to generators spinning in perfect step across a whole country.

chapters.title: Flight
chapters.tease: The Wright brothers' first flight was shorter than the wingspan of a jumbo jet.

chapters.title: Medicine
chapters.tease: Smallpox killed hundreds of millions of people; it is now the only human disease ever eradicated.

chapters.title: Computers
chapters.tease: Ada Lovelace published a program in 1843 for a computer that was never built.

chapters.title: The Internet
chapters.tease: The first message sent across the internet's ancestor was 'LO', because the computer crashed.

chapters.title: Artificial Intelligence
chapters.tease: Instead of being given rules, a learning machine is shown examples and works out the rules itself.

chapters.title: Human Origins
chapters.tease: Every human alive descends from a few thousand Africans who set out around 60,000 years ago.

chapters.title: The First Farmers
chapters.tease: For 95% of our history humans foraged. Then, about 12,000 years ago, they began to plant.

chapters.title: Mesopotamia
chapters.tease: Writing was invented in Mesopotamia not for poetry but to count sheep, grain and beer.

chapters.title: Ancient Egypt
chapters.tease: The Great Pyramid was the world's tallest building for nearly 4,000 years, and slaves did not build it.

chapters.title: Ancient Greece
chapters.tease: Athenians chose most officials by lottery, convinced that elections favoured the rich.

chapters.title: Ancient Rome
chapters.tease: Julius Caesar was never an emperor; the first was his adopted heir, Augustus, in 27 BCE.

chapters.title: Ancient China
chapters.tease: Chinese writing has been in continuous use for over 3,000 years, since the Shang oracle bones.

chapters.title: Ancient India
chapters.tease: Mohenjo-daro had covered street drains 4,500 years ago, and its script is still unread.

chapters.title: The Ancient Americas
chapters.tease: Aztec Tenochtitlan, built on a lake, was larger than almost any city in Europe in 1519.

chapters.title: The Silk Roads
chapters.tease: Almost nobody travelled the whole Silk Road; goods, ideas and germs went hand to hand across Asia.

chapters.part: The Making of the Modern World
chapters.title: The Medieval World
chapters.tease: In four years the Black Death killed perhaps a third to a half of everyone in Europe.

chapters.part: The Making of the Modern World
chapters.title: The Islamic Golden Age
chapters.tease: The word algorithm comes from the name of a ninth-century Baghdad mathematician, al-Khwarizmi.

chapters.part: The Making of the Modern World
chapters.title: The Renaissance
chapters.tease: Brunelleschi's dome in Florence, finished in 1436, is still the largest brick dome ever built.

chapters.part: The Making of the Modern World
chapters.title: The Age of Exploration
chapters.tease: Magellan's fleet set out with five ships; one ship and 18 men made it all the way round the world.

chapters.part: The Making of the Modern World
chapters.title: The Scientific Revolution
chapters.tease: Newton showed that the force pulling an apple down is the same one that keeps the Moon in orbit.

chapters.part: The Making of the Modern World
chapters.title: The Industrial Revolution
chapters.tease: By 1851 most Britons lived in towns, the first time this had happened in any large country.

chapters.part: The Making of the Modern World
chapters.title: Revolutions and Rights
chapters.tease: When crowds stormed the Bastille in 1789, the hated prison held just seven prisoners.

chapters.part: The Making of the Modern World
chapters.title: The World Wars
chapters.tease: On a single day at the Somme in 1916, the British Army suffered about 57,000 casualties.

chapters.part: The Making of the Modern World
chapters.title: The Cold War
chapters.tease: In 1962 Soviet missiles sat in Cuba, 150 km from Florida, and the world waited thirteen days.

chapters.part: The Making of the Modern World
chapters.title: The Global Age
chapters.tease: In 1950 Earth held 2.5 billion people; in 2022 the UN welcomed the eight billionth.

chapters.title: Languages
chapters.tease: Papua New Guinea, home to about ten million people, speaks around 840 different languages.

chapters.title: Writing
chapters.tease: Writing was invented from scratch only a few times, and the first texts were accounts of barley and beer.

chapters.title: Literature
chapters.tease: The first author known by name was a woman, the priestess Enheduanna, writing over 4,300 years ago.

chapters.title: Painting
chapters.tease: The oldest known painting, a life-size pig on a cave wall in Sulawesi, is at least 45,500 years old.

chapters.title: Architecture
chapters.tease: The Great Pyramid stayed the tallest human-made structure on Earth for about 3,800 years.

chapters.title: Music
chapters.tease: Bone flutes from German caves show that humans were making music around 40,000 years ago.

chapters.title: Theatre and Film
chapters.tease: Greek theatres seated up to 14,000 people, and an actor's voice reached the back row unamplified.

chapters.title: World Religions
chapters.tease: About three in every four people alive today identify with a religion.

chapters.title: Myths and Legends
chapters.tease: One folk tale, The Smith and the Devil, may have been told and retold for around 6,000 years.

chapters.title: Sport and Games
chapters.tease: Football's first written laws came in 1863; its rough ancestor pitted whole villages against each other.

chapters.title: Numbers
chapters.tease: Nothing was humanity's hardest number to invent: zero took thousands of years to arrive.

chapters.title: Measuring Time
chapters.tease: In 1752 Britain went to bed on 2 September and woke up on 14 September.

chapters.title: Maps
chapters.tease: On most wall maps Greenland looks as big as Africa. Africa is about fourteen times larger.

chapters.title: Money and Trade
chapters.tease: Some stone money on the island of Yap was too heavy to move; owners simply agreed who held it.

chapters.title: Government
chapters.tease: Ancient Athens chose most of its officials by lottery, fearing that elections favoured the rich.

chapters.title: Law and Rights
chapters.tease: Magna Carta, sealed in 1215 to bind a king, was annulled by the Pope within about ten weeks.

chapters.title: Philosophy
chapters.tease: Socrates, the most famous philosopher of all, never wrote down a single word.

chapters.title: The Scientific Method
chapters.tease: Handwashing cut deaths on a Vienna maternity ward tenfold in 1847, and doctors still scoffed.

chapters.title: Cities
chapters.tease: Around 2007, for the first time, more humans lived in towns and cities than in the countryside.

chapters.title: The Story of Knowledge
chapters.tease: The Yongle Encyclopedia of 1408 filled 11,095 volumes and was so vast it was never printed.
